title: Clearing a fallen tree from a road or yard
summary: How to cut up a tree that wind or ice has brought down without it killing you: read the tension before every cut, deal with what hangs overhead first and from a distance, keep the bar nose off everything, and never work alone. Spring poles, rolling trunks, root plates, hung-up trees, kickback and live wires are how people die doing this.

materials.item: Chainsaw with a working chain brake and a sharp chain, or a bow saw or crosscut saw for small stuff
Chainsaw chaps or trousers with cut-retardant pads, labelled to a standard
Mesh face screen or face shield, worn over safety glasses
Ear muffs, with foam plugs under them for long sessions
Boots with chainsaw protection (green fir tree on a white label), or steel-toed boots with non-slip soles
Plastic felling wedges and a hammer or axe to drive them
First-aid kit with a tourniquet and pressure dressings

steps.text: Stand back and look up and round the whole tree: hung trees, hanging limbs, broken tops, ice, and every wire (USFS chain saw course, OSHA chainsaws).
steps.warn: Any wire in or near the tree: treat it as live, stay 10 m (33 ft) back and leave that tree (OSHA trim, BC Hydro, Manitoba Hydro).

steps.text: Wait out wind, ice and poor light. Clean up after the ice and snow have melted, in daylight (NC State winter, STIHL MS 162/172).
steps.warn: Ice and dead limbs fall as the air warms, sometimes days later (see the falling ice card).

steps.text: Bring a partner who stays out of the hazard area and can stop bleeding and go for help. Check on each other at least every half hour (WorkSafeBC Part 26, OSHA chainsaws).
Put on chaps or cut-resistant trousers, a helmet with a face screen and ear muffs, safety glasses, gloves and chainsaw boots (OSHA chainsaws, STIHL MS 162/172, WorkSafeBC Part 8).

Check the saw: chain brake works, chain sharp and properly tensioned. Fuel it 3 m (10 ft) from any flame, then start it 3 m from the fuelling spot, on the ground with the brake on (OSHA 1910.266, OSHA chainsaws).
steps.warn: Never drop-start a saw or run it indoors: its exhaust carries carbon monoxide (OSHA 1910.266, STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: Clear brush from your footing and plan two ways out, with room to step back at least 2.4 m (8 ft) on the final cut (USFS chain saw course).

Deal with hung trees and hanging limbs first, from outside their reach. OSHA's answer is a machine that pushes or pulls them down while nobody stands under them (OSHA eTool hazards, Manitoba G-20). Without one, mark the tree and keep at least two tree lengths away (OSHA 1910.266).
steps.warn: Never work under a hung tree or limb. Don't cut the tree holding it up, and don't fell another tree onto it (Manitoba G-20).

steps.text: Limb the tree first so you can see where the trunk is under strain. Stand uphill, on the side of the log away from the limb you cut, and leave the limbs that prop the log until last (STIHL MS 162/172, Husqvarna after the storm).
steps.warn: Keep the bar nose off everything: that's where kickback starts. Never cut above shoulder height or standing on the log (STIHL MS 162/172).

steps.text: Spring poles: leave them if you can. If not, make 4 to 6 shallow cuts 12 mm (1/2 in) apart on the inside (under side) of the bend, stopping as soon as it moves, then release it from the other side (USFS chain saw course).
steps.warn: Stand clear of the end that will spring. Nobody else within two tree lengths (OSHA 1910.266).

steps.text: Read the bind on each trunk cut: a small relieving cut on the squeezed side first, then finish from the stretched side; wedge the cut open (STIHL MS 162/172, USFS chain saw course).
steps.warn: Where the trunk lies bent under heavy strain, stand on the inside of the curve and cut a little at a time from both sides (Husqvarna trees under tension).

steps.text: Work from the top end toward the roots, one cut at a time, and drag each piece clear before cutting it up (USFS instructor, STIHL MS 162/172).
If the bar is pinched, shut the engine off and set the brake before you free it, then wedge the cut open (STIHL MS 162/172).
steps.warn: The limb or log can snap or release as it lets go of the bar.

steps.text: Cut the trunk off the root plate last, about 0.5 m (20 in) up the trunk, with the root plate on your left and the cut to your right, and only if the tree can't turn over (Husqvarna after the storm).
steps.warn: The trunk can kick out sideways when it is cut through, and a root plate left upright can fall on people. Keep the way behind you clear (Husqvarna after the storm).

steps.text: Stop when you are tired: more kickbacks, pinched bars and near misses are the sign (USFS chain saw course). Leave what you can't do safely, marked, for another day.

notes:
## What goes wrong
A wind-thrown tree lies bent over stumps, rocks and other trees, with much of its wood in tension or compression. Cut it and limbs can spring out and the trunk can jump, roll or pinch the saw (Husqvarna after the storm, STIHL MS 162/172). How people get hurt:
- **Spring poles:** saplings and limbs pinned under the trunk spring back when cut. Many professional loggers have been hurt this way (OSHA trim).
- **The trunk:** a cut can let it drop, roll or swing (STIHL MS 162/172).
- **The root plate:** Husqvarna says to cut the root by hand only when there is no risk of the uprooted tree turning over, and not to leave an uprooted tree standing upright where it could fall on people (Husqvarna after the storm).
- **Overhead:** trees hung up in other trees, broken limbs hanging loose (widow-makers), snapped tops and ice. OSHA tells loggers not to work near a hung (lodged) tree at all until a machine has pushed or pulled it down (OSHA eTool hazards).
- **Kickback:** the bar nose touches something and the saw flies up and back at you (STIHL MS 162/172).
- **Wires** tangled in the branches, and **being tired or alone**.

## Before the first cut
- Walk round it from a distance and look up: hung trees, hanging limbs, broken tops, ice (USFS chain saw course).
- Find every wire before you go near (OSHA chainsaws). Look for nails, fence wire and spikes in yard trees too (OSHA chainsaws, STIHL MS 162/172).
- Wind, fog, rain or poor light: wait for good daylight (STIHL MS 162/172).
- A partner, out of the hazard area, who can shut a saw off, stop bleeding and go for help. WorkSafeBC makes forestry employers check on every faller and bucker at least every half hour and give them a way to call for help (WorkSafeBC Part 26); OSHA says never work alone (OSHA chainsaws).
- Everyone else stays well back: all workers clear of the hazard area before anything is bucked (WorkSafeBC Part 26), and for felling at least twice the height of the trees (OSHA chainsaws).
- Plan two ways out and clear them of brush; leave yourself more than 2.4 m (8 ft) of room to step back on the final cut (USFS chain saw course).

## Power lines
Assume every line is live (OSHA trim). Stay at least 10 m (33 ft) back from a downed line (BC Hydro). A tree touching a line can be live, so keep that distance from it and from anything the line touches (Manitoba Hydro, [high-voltage card](#browse/hazards/hv)). Don't touch limbs that may touch a line, and don't do tree work where wires are involved (NC State winter, STIHL MS 162/172). A generator feeding a building can make dead lines live again (high-voltage card). Leave that tree: cut round it, mark it and keep people away.

## Ice and dead wood
Wait until the ice and snow have melted before you clean up (NC State winter); stay away from big ice-laden trees (Iowa State ice) and from hanging branches and split trunks (Forests Canada ice). Ice comes off as the air warms toward 0 °C, sometimes days after the storm (see the [falling ice card](#browse/hazards/ice_fall)). Ash killed by emerald ash borer is brittle: big limbs snap 9 m (30 ft) up on a calm day (Purdue ash).

## Gear
| Item | What to look for | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Leg protection | Chaps or trousers with cut-retardant pads covering the whole thigh down to the boot, overlapping the boots by 5 cm (2 in). BC's workplace rules require them for any worker running a chainsaw, with a permanently attached label naming the standard | OSHA 1910.266, USFS instructor, WorkSafeBC Part 8 |
| Helmet | Approved hard hat | STIHL MS 162/172 |
| Eyes and face | Close-fitting safety glasses marked CSA Z94, with a face screen over them; mesh logger screens are allowed | STIHL MS 162/172, OSHA 1910.266 |
| Hearing | Muffs or plugs; both together for chainsaws | OSHA chainsaws, noise card |
| Gloves | Work gloves | STIHL MS 162/172, OSHA chainsaws |
| Boots | White label with a green fir tree means chainsaw protection (CSA); otherwise sturdy steel-toed boots with non-slip soles | CCOHS footwear, STIHL MS 162/172 |
| High-visibility vest or jacket | Husqvarna lists a fluorescent jacket for storm work | Husqvarna after the storm |

Where to find and check them: [boots](#browse/parts/ppe_boots_safety), [hard hats](#browse/parts/ppe_hard_hat), [face screens](#browse/parts/ppe_face_shield), [glasses](#browse/parts/ppe_safety_glasses), [muffs](#browse/parts/ppe_earmuffs), [plugs](#browse/parts/ppe_earplugs), [gloves](#browse/parts/ppe_gloves_leather), [hi-vis](#browse/parts/ppe_hi_vis).

## The saw
- A working chain brake, a sharp, properly tensioned chain, and a low-kickback chain and bar (STIHL MS 162/172, OSHA chainsaws). See [Chainsaw chain](#guides/skill_chainsaw_chain) and [Fix a chainsaw](#guides/repair_chainsaw).
- Fuel it at least 3 m (10 ft) from any flame and start it at least 3 m from where you fuelled it, on the ground with the brake on; never drop-start it (OSHA 1910.266, OSHA chainsaws).
- Both hands, thumbs wrapped round the handles (OSHA 1910.266). Never above shoulder height, never from a ladder or a log, never overreaching (STIHL MS 162/172).
- Keep the bar nose off everything: kickback starts when the chain at the top of the nose touches wood or is pinched (STIHL MS 162/172).
- Brake on whenever you move (USFS chain saw course). Never run it indoors: its exhaust carries carbon monoxide (STIHL MS 162/172).
- Tiredness shows as more kickbacks, pinched bars and near misses (USFS chain saw course). Stop then.

## Reading the bind
Watch the cut: if it closes, the top is squeezed; if it opens, the bottom is (USFS chain saw course). Make a small relieving cut on the squeezed (compression) side first, then finish from the stretched (tension) side (STIHL MS 162/172, USFS chain saw course).

| Bind | Squeezed side | First cut | Finish |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top bind | Top | Small cut from the top | From below |
| Bottom bind | Bottom | Small cut from below | From the top |
| Side bind | One side | Squeezed side | Stretched side |
| End bind (weight compresses the whole cross-section) | Whole cross-section | From the top, with a wedge in early | Down through |

Source: USFS chain saw course. Logs often carry two binds at once (USFS chain saw course). Use plastic felling wedges to hold the cut open (STIHL MS 162/172). Where a trunk lies bent under heavy strain, stand on the inside of the curve and cut a little at a time from both sides (Husqvarna trees under tension).

## Spring poles
Leave them if you can (USFS chain saw course). If one must go: stand well back and make four to six shallow cuts about 12 mm (1/2 in) apart on the inside (under side) of the bend, stopping each the moment the wood moves, then release it from the other side, clear of the piece that will spring (USFS chain saw course). Nobody but the cutter within two tree lengths when it lets go (OSHA 1910.266). More in [Lines under load](#browse/hazards/line_recoil).

## Hung-up trees and widow-makers
OSHA's answer is a machine: push or pull a hung tree down, and knock or pull hanging limbs down, without working under them (OSHA eTool hazards). If a hung tree stays up, mark it and do no work within two tree lengths of it (OSHA 1910.266). Don't fell another tree onto it and don't cut the tree that is holding it up (Manitoba G-20). Manitoba's workplace guideline lets a tractor or portable winch pull a hard hang-up down, but only from equipment with an operator protective structure, never on a side slope, using a heavy chain at least 1.5 times as long as the tree, not rope (Manitoba G-20). We found no source for pulling a hung tree down with a car, or with a rope and a hand winch, and a line under load can recoil ([Lines under load](#browse/hazards/line_recoil)); without that kind of machine, leave the tree up, marked.

## Cutting order
1. Hanging trees and limbs first, brought down by a machine or left marked and avoided (OSHA eTool hazards, Husqvarna after the storm).
2. Limb it, so you can see where the trunk is under strain (Husqvarna after the storm). Stand on the side of the log away from the limb, uphill, and never on the log (STIHL MS 162/172). Leave the limbs propping the log until last, so it can't roll (STIHL MS 162/172).
3. Drag cut pieces out to a clear spot before cutting them up; cut one log at a time, never into a pile (STIHL MS 162/172).
4. Cut the trunk from the top end toward the roots (USFS instructor, Husqvarna after the storm).
5. Root plate last. Cut the trunk about 0.5 m (20 in) up from the roots, standing with the root plate on your left and cutting to your right, only if the tree can't turn over, and keep the way behind you clear because the trunk can kick out sideways (Husqvarna after the storm).

On a road, clear the lane you need and leave the rest: less cutting is less exposure.

## When no help is coming
- **Saw cut:** saw off, brake on, firm direct pressure. Bleeding from an arm or leg that pressure won't stop needs a tourniquet: see [Severe bleeding](#ref/reference_first_aid/severe_bleeding) and the first aid on the [lines-under-load card](#browse/hazards/line_recoil).
- **Someone pinned under a trunk:** shut the saw off first. Where you can, lift rather than cut: a bar or jack with blocks slid under as it rises (see the [crush card](#browse/hazards/crush)), because cutting a loaded trunk can make it drop or roll (STIHL MS 162/172).
- **Hit on the head by a limb:** keep them still and watch for confusion, drowsiness or vomiting (lines-under-load card).
- **A wire in the tree:** leave it all. If someone is touching it, don't touch them; stay 10 m back (high-voltage card).
- **Bar pinched:** engine off and brake on before you try to free it, and watch for the limb to snap or release; then wedge the cut open (STIHL MS 162/172).
- **Too big, too bent or hung up:** leave it. Cut a way round, mark it, and keep everyone at least two tree lengths away for as long as it stays up (OSHA 1910.266, Manitoba G-20).
